slides.text:
An array is a numbered row of values of one type, with a length that is fixed when you write it. It is the plain building block that Go's flexible lists are made from.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
row of 3 numbers
    position 0, position 1, position 2

slides.text:
Three sessions:

- **Session 1:** declaring arrays, reading and changing positions, and walking them
- **Session 2:** arrays as values you copy, compare and pass to functions
- **Session 3:** indexed literals, grids and counting with an index

Every position has an index, and counting starts at 0. An array of 3 has the indexes 0, 1 and 2, and nothing else.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
scores = row of 3 numbers
scores at 0 = 90
read scores at 2

slides.text: The length is written in the type, and it can never grow or shrink. A position that was never set holds the zero value of the type.

exercises.title: Declare an array
exercises.guide: Make an array and fill its positions.

chunks.guide: An array has a fixed length, written in brackets before the type. Without values, every position starts at the zero value.

notes.text: The 3 is the length, and it never changes.

chunks.guide: A position is picked with its index in brackets. The first one is 0.

exercises.title: Start with values
exercises.guide: Write an array with its values already inside.

chunks.guide: A literal lists the values in braces after the type.

notes.text: Four ints, so four values go in the braces.

chunks.guide: Printing an array shows its values in brackets. The last of four is at index 3.
`len` tells how many positions the array has.

exercises.title: Let Go count
exercises.guide: Write an array without saying its length.

chunks.guide: With `...` in place of the length, Go counts the values for you. The array still has a fixed length.

notes.text: Go fills in the 3 from the values.

chunks.guide: Assigning to a position replaces the value there.

exercises.title: Count and replace
exercises.guide: Print how many names the array holds, then replace the second one.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var stock [4]int
    stock[2] = 6
    stock[3] = stock[2] + 1
    fmt.Println(stock, len(stock))
}
exercises.explanation: Positions start at 0, so index 2 is the third one. Unset positions stay 0, and `len` is the length of the array, 4.

exercises.title: Walk an array
exercises.guide: Visit every position of an array with range.

chunks.guide: A list of temperatures and a total to grow.
`range` gives the index and the value of each position, as it did with a string.
This line runs after the loop.

slides.text:
An array behaves like a number: when you assign it or pass it to a function, the whole row is copied. Changing the copy leaves the original alone.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
b = copy of a
change b at 0
a is untouched

slides.text: The length is part of the type, so an array of 3 ints and an array of 4 ints are different types. Two arrays of the same type can be compared with `==`.

exercises.title: Assign an array
exercises.guide: Give an array to a new variable, then change the new one.

chunks.guide: Assigning an array to another variable copies every value.

notes.text: Not a link: b gets its own values.

chunks.guide: Only `b` changes. `a` keeps its values.

exercises.title: Compare arrays
exercises.guide: Check whether two arrays hold the same values.

chunks.guide: Three arrays of the same type. Two hold the same values, in the same order.
`==` compares the values one by one, in order.

exercises.title: Send an array in
exercises.guide: Pass an array to a function and see what comes back.

chunks.guide: The parameter type includes the length. The function gets a copy of the array, so it changes only its own.

notes.text: Only a [3]int fits here, not a [4]int.

chunks.guide: The array in `main` is the same as before the call.

exercises.title: Copy and compare
exercises.guide: Copy `a` into `b`, change `b`, then print whether the two are equal.

exercises.title: Why does it not compile?
exercises.guide: Read the message, then pick the cause.
exercises.code:
./main.go:8:7: cannot use b (variable of
type [4]int) as [3]int value in
assignment
options: An array cannot be assigned to a variable
The two arrays have different lengths
`b` needs the `...` length to be copied
exercises.explanation: The length is part of the type, so [4]int and [3]int are two different types and one cannot take the other.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `b` is a copy, so changing `a` does not reach it. They are no longer equal, and `b[1]` is still 2.

slides.text:
A literal can name the positions it fills, and every other position stays at its zero value. A grid is an array whose items are arrays.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
row of 5 numbers
    position 1 = 10
    position 3 = 30

grid of 2 rows, 3 columns
    cell at row 1, column 2

slides.text: A fixed length is a good fit for a fixed set of things, like one counter per letter of the alphabet. An integer value, such as a letter minus `'a'`, works as an index.

exercises.title: Fill chosen positions
exercises.guide: Write literals that set only some positions.

chunks.guide: Fewer values than the length is fine. The positions left over keep the zero value.
An index and a colon before a value put it in that position.
With `...` the length reaches the highest position named.

exercises.title: Build a grid
exercises.guide: An array of arrays, filled with nested loops.

chunks.guide: Two lengths make a grid: 2 rows, each with 3 ints.
The outer loop walks the rows and the inner one the columns. Two indexes pick a cell.
`len` of the grid counts rows, and `len` of one row counts columns.

exercises.title: Count letters
exercises.guide: Use letters as indexes into an array of counters.

chunks.guide: One counter for each of the 26 letters.
A letter minus `'a'` is its place in the alphabet, so it works as the index.
Read the counters of `h` and `l`.

exercises.title: Sum without the index
exercises.guide: Add up the prices without using their positions, then print the total and how many prices there are.
